lesson.title: Finding the Overlap: Set Intersection
lesson.summary: The & operator (or the .intersection() method) builds a new set containing only the elements two sets have in common.
lesson.body:
The Set Operations chapter introduced the union operator, |, which combines everything from two sets into one, dropping duplicates along the way. Union answers "what do we have if we put both groups together." Intersection asks a narrower and often more useful question: "what do these two groups share." If you have a set of students enrolled in a morning study session and another set enrolled in a weekend session, the intersection tells you exactly who shows up to both, without writing a single loop.

In Python, the & operator computes the intersection of two sets, and the .intersection() method does the same thing with method syntax. Both return a brand new set; neither original set is changed. Conceptually this matches the overlapping region of a Venn diagram: an element ends up in the result only if it exists in every set involved.

morning_shift = {"Alicia", "Bao", "Carmen", "Deion"}
weekend_shift = {"Bao", "Deion", "Elif"}

overlap = morning_shift & weekend_shift
print(sorted(overlap))
print(morning_shift.intersection(weekend_shift) == overlap)

This prints ['Bao', 'Deion'] followed by True. Notice the sorted() call around the printed set. Sets store elements by hash value, not by the order you inserted them, and Python randomizes string hashing between runs for security reasons, so printing a raw set of strings can display its elements in a different order each time you run the program. Wrapping the result in sorted() gives a predictable, readable list for output, without changing what the set itself actually contains.

Intersection scales far better than the naive alternative of writing a nested loop to compare every name in one list against every name in another. Because sets are built on hash tables, checking whether an element belongs to a set takes roughly constant time on average, so computing an intersection takes time proportional to the size of the smaller set rather than the product of both sizes. You can also intersect more than two sets at once, either by chaining the operator, a & b & c, or by passing multiple arguments to the method, a.intersection(b, c). If two sets share nothing at all, the intersection is simply an empty set, not an error.
